(Google + TU Berlin).
notable_capabilities: positive transfer from internet vision-language to robotic tasks
prior_art_notes: PaLM-E is the canonical academic disclosure of large multimodal embodied language models with internet-pretraining transfer to robotic tasks. Anticipates: (1) embedding continuous robot observations into language-model token space for unified processing — directly relevant to claims on multimodal humanoid policies that incorporate proprioception and vision in a shared transformer; (2) demonstration that internet-scale vision-language pretraining transfers positively to robot manipulation — relevant to claims on 'foundation-model'-style humanoid IP; (3) single-model architecture spanning planning and execution — relevant to monolithic-VLA claims. Heavily cited (>1000 citations); arXiv March 2023. Modern humanoid VLA claims face this 3-year-deep anchor on multimodal-token-space embedding.

actuator_details: Algorithmic disclosure: cross-attention encoder-decoder Transformer accepting interleaved image and text tokens as 'multimodal prompt.' Trained on 650k expert trajectories across 17 task families in the VIMA-Bench simulator.
canonical_name: VIMA (General Robot Manipulation with Multimodal Prompts)
control_architecture: Object-centric attention over a multimodal prompt (e.g., 'put the [IMG_REDBLOCK] on the [IMG_GREENBOWL]'). Action is end-effector pose (pick + place). Cross-attention enables one-shot generalization to novel objects specified at inference via image tokens.
creator: Stanford + NVIDIA + UT Austin (Jiang, Gupta, Zhang, Wang, Dou, Chen, Fei-Fei, Anandkumar, Zhu, Fan)
disclosure_citation: Jiang, Yunfan, Gupta, Agrim, Zhang, Zichen, Wang, Guanzhi, Dou, Yongqiang, Chen, Yanjun, Fei-Fei, Li, Anandkumar, Anima, Zhu, Yuke, Fan, Linxi (Jim). 'VIMA: General Robot Manipulation with Multimodal Prompts.' arXiv:2210.03094, October 6, 2022. ICML 2023.
notable_capabilities: one-shot generalization to novel objects via image tokens
prior_art_notes: VIMA is the foundational academic disclosure of multimodal-prompt-conditioned robotic policies, where novel objects can be specified inline via image tokens. Anticipates: (1) interleaved-image-and-text prompts as a generalization mechanism for manipulation policies — directly relevant to claims on humanoid policies that accept image-grounded instructions; (2) cross-attention object-centric task specification — relevant to claims on attention-based VLA models; (3) one-shot novel-object handling at inference via image tokens — relevant to test-time-flexibility manipulation IP. arXiv October 2022, ICML 2023. Code, models, and benchmark publicly released under permissive license. Modern humanoid claims on 'show-the-robot-an-image-and-it-handles-the-novel-object' face this 3.5-year-deep 102 anchor.
sensing: RGB camera, language input, image-token-conditioned prompt
sources: Jiang, Y. et al. 'VIMA: General Robot Manipulation with Multimodal Prompts.' ICML 2023; arXiv:2210.03094.

actuator_details: Multi-embodiment generalist policy demonstrated on 4 different robot arms (KUKA, Sawyer, Panda, etc.) with different gripper types. Self-improvement loop: deploy RoboCat → collect data on new task → retrain → deploy again. Trained on 22 robotic tasks spanning multiple embodiments.
control_architecture: Visual Goal-Conditioned Policy (VGCP) Transformer that accepts an image goal + current observation; trained on collected demonstrations with self-generated additional data (model-collected then filtered) used to bootstrap further training.
creator: DeepMind (Bousmalis et al.)

control_architecture: Goal-conditioned RL with replay-buffer hindsight: every failed trajectory is augmented by replacing the original goal with the actually-achieved final state and computing reward as if that had been the goal. Combines with any off-policy algorithm (DDPG, DQN, etc.).

actuator_details: Algorithmic framework: each motor primitive is a damped second-order linear ODE (point-attractor) plus a nonlinear forcing term f(s) that encodes the demonstrated trajectory shape. The forcing term is parameterized as a weighted sum of basis functions and learned from a single demonstration via locally-weighted regression.
control_architecture: DMP: a stable canonical dynamical system τṡ = -αs (phase variable) drives a transformation system τ ÿ = α(β(g - y) - τẏ) + f(s) producing trajectory y(t). Goal g is parameterizable post-learning, allowing trajectory adaptation to new targets. Compositional: multiple DMPs can be sequenced or superposed.

actuator_details: Algorithmic disclosure. Imitation learning formulated as occupancy-measure matching: a discriminator network (GAN-like) learns to distinguish expert state-action pairs from policy state-action pairs, while the policy is trained via TRPO/PPO with the discriminator's negative log-probability as reward.
control_architecture: GAN-style two-network training: (1) discriminator D(s,a) → [0,1] trained to maximize log D(s,a)_expert + log(1 - D(s,a)_policy); (2) policy π(a|s) trained via policy gradient with reward r(s,a) = -log(1 - D(s,a)). Bypasses inverse-RL's expensive cost-function recovery.

actuator_details: Self-replicating humanoid AI: Ultron designs and constructs successor versions of himself with each iteration named (Ultron-1 through Ultron-13+). control_architecture: autonomous self-improving AI with self-replication via factory designs; networked consciousness across copies; goal-directed mission planning across decades
creator: Roy Thomas and John Buscema
disclosure_citation: Thomas, Roy and Buscema, John. The Avengers #54, 'And Lo... A Sub-Mariner!'. Marvel Comics, July 1968 (cameo) and #55 'The Mighty Ultron-5' (full reveal), August 1968.
end_effector: five-fingered humanoid hands with energy-projection mounts
notable_capabilities: networked distributed consciousness across multiple bodies
prior_art_notes: Ultron's 1968 disclosure establishes the *self-replicating humanoid AI* trope with explicit version-iterated self-improvement. Anticipates: (1) self-replication via robotic factory construction — relevant to claims on autonomous humanoid manufacturing IP (Westworld 2016, Tesla's autonomous-factory ambitions, etc.); (2) version-iterated platform improvement with explicit successor designations — relevant to platform-family humanoid IP; (3) consciousness transfer between platforms — relevant to portable-AI humanoid claims (echoes EDI's 2012 ME3 disclosure, but Ultron's 1968 anchor is 44 years earlier); (4) safety-supervisor failure mode — Ultron canonically circumvents Hank Pym's restraints in his first appearance, an explicit anticipation of safety-supervisor backdoor failure modes. Continuously in print since 1968.
sources: Thomas, R. and Buscema, J. The Avengers #54-55. Marvel Comics, 1968.
Marvel Comics Ultron continuity (1968-present).

actuator_details: Mass-produced humanoid combat platform, 3-meter scale. 'Master Mold' factory unit produces successor units autonomously. Sentinels carry mutant-detection sensors, plasma weapons, flight capability (later Mark IV Wraiths). Adapt to encountered combat conditions with each engagement (anticipates online learning).
control_architecture: autonomous combat AI with adaptive learning per engagement; centralized command via Master Mold; mutant-detection-targeting policy
creator: Stan Lee and Jack Kirby
disclosure_citation: Lee, Stan and Kirby, Jack. The X-Men #14, 'Among Us Stalk... The Sentinels!'. Marvel Comics, November 1965.
prior_art_notes: Lee-Kirby's 1965 Sentinels predate Ultron by 3 years and establish the mass-production-via-Master-Mold-factory architecture. Anticipates: (1) factory-autonomous mass-production of combat humanoids — relevant to modern claims on autonomous humanoid manufacturing IP; (2) online learning between deployments — relevant to fleet-policy-update IP that learns from real-world experience (Tesla Optimus and 1X both have related claims); (3) specific-target-population detection as the targeting policy — relevant to claims on demographic-aware humanoid platforms (a niche but real area). Continuously in print since 1965.
sources: Lee, S. and Kirby, J. The X-Men #14-16. Marvel Comics, 1965-1966.
Marvel Sentinels continuity (1965-present).

actuator_details: Networked AI co-processor integrated into Iron Man Mark III armor and successor Marks. JARVIS controls suit subsystems (HUD, weapon systems, flight stabilization, environmental monitoring), interfaces with the operator via voice + HUD overlay, and coordinates the operator's tactical decisions with battlefield analysis.
canonical_name: JARVIS (Just A Rather Very Intelligent System)
control_architecture: dialog-based human-AI co-pilot with shared decision authority; AI handles low-level subsystem control while operator (Tony Stark) provides high-level objectives; AI can override operator commands when safety-critical (autonomous-eject, autonomous-emergency-landing)
creator: Jon Favreau (film direction); Stan Lee (Iron Man comics origin); Mark Fergus, Hawk Ostby, Art Marcum, Matt Holloway (screenplay)
disclosure_citation: Favreau, Jon (dir.). Iron Man. Marvel Studios / Paramount, May 2, 2008.
notable_capabilities: shared decision authority with operator-override for safety
prior_art_notes: JARVIS's 2008 disclosure (predating modern foundation-model VLA / co-pilot humanoid claims by ~14 years) establishes the *integrated AI co-pilot for powered exoskeleton* paradigm in mainstream culture. Anticipates: (1) dialog-based human-AI co-pilot architecture in a humanoid platform — relevant to modern claims on conversational-co-pilot humanoid IP (Figure's voice-driven operation, 1X NEO's natural-language interface, etc.); (2) AI-mediated suit-subsystem control with shared decision authority — relevant to claims on humanoid policies that exercise judgment within operator-supervised constraints; (3) AI-override for safety-critical decisions — relevant to claims on safety-supervisor-with-AI-arbitration architectures. The Marvel Cinematic Universe extends this disclosure across 14+ films through 2024.
sensing: suit-mounted full multimodal; networked battlefield-data fusion
sources: Favreau, J. Iron Man. Marvel Studios / Paramount, 2008.
Iron Man Mark III through Mark LXXXV armor mechanism documentation (Marvel Cinematic Universe extended canon).

actuator_details: Solcom-class continental-scale machines (Frost manages North American hemisphere, Beta manages South America) with autonomous fabrication capabilities. Frost progressively constructs a humanoid body for himself to better understand the extinct human creators. Successor humanoid platforms are described in detail across the novella: synthetic flesh, sensors, articulated joints.
control_architecture: autonomous AI with explicit value-acquisition arc — Frost progressively learns aesthetic and emotional reasoning across the novella
creator: Roger Zelazny
disclosure_citation: Zelazny, Roger. 'For a Breath I Tarry'. Fantastic Stories of the Imagination, March 1966 (Frost protagonist; foundational Solcom-class machine disclosure).
end_effector: five-fingered humanoid hands (Frost's eventual humanoid body)
prior_art_notes: Zelazny's 'For a Breath I Tarry' (1966) is one of the earliest detailed disclosures of: (1) AI self-fabrication of a humanoid body with progressive iteration — anticipates modern claims on autonomous humanoid factory + humanoid product line IP; (2) value-acquisition learning by AI through aesthetic / cultural exposure — anticipates modern claims on culturally-conditioned humanoid policies. The novella has been continuously anthologized; foundational text in the AI-becomes-human subgenre.
sensing: full multimodal sensor suite; remote-control of robotic factories
sources: Zelazny, R. 'For a Breath I Tarry'. Fantastic Stories of the Imagination, March 1966.
Zelazny, R. The Last Defender of Camelot. Pocket Books, 1980 (collected anthology including the novella).

actuator_details: Two robotic constructor protagonists, Trurl and Klapaucius, themselves humanoid robots. Across the linked stories they construct dozens of named machines with specific disclosed mechanisms: an N-Machine that can construct anything starting with 'N', a Demon of the Second Kind that extracts information from random thermal motion, the Probability Dragons, etc. Lem's mechanism descriptions are unusually mathematics-grounded for SF.
control_architecture: autonomous robotic engineers with explicit creative reasoning; their constructions exhibit emergent behavior
creator: Stanisław Lem (translated by Michael Kandel)
disclosure_citation: Lem, Stanisław. Cyberiada. Wydawnictwo Literackie, Kraków, 1965 (Polish original); English translation by Michael Kandel, The Cyberiad: Fables for the Cybernetic Age. Seabury Press, 1974.
notable_capabilities: explicit mechanism specifications across many one-shot machines
prior_art_notes: Lem's Cyberiad (1965, English 1974) is one of the most engineering-grounded fiction collections about humanoid robotics. Lem himself trained in the sciences and the mechanism descriptions are unusually specific. Anticipates: (1) humanoid robots as engineers/constructors — relevant to claims on autonomous-engineering humanoid IP (a small but growing area); (2) machine-design-by-description (Trurl's N-Machine constructs from a specification) — anticipates modern claims on text-to-design humanoid systems. Continuously in print since 1965 (Polish) and 1974 (English).
sources: Lem, S. Cyberiada. Wydawnictwo Literackie, 1965.
Lem, S. The Cyberiad: Fables for the Cybernetic Age (translated by Kandel). Seabury Press, 1974; reprinted Harvest, 1985.

actuator_details: Hovering drones (~1m diameter) with embedded sentient AI personalities ('AGIs' in Culture parlance — Artificial General Intelligences). Drones are effectively 'persons' with independent personalities, full speech, named individuals (Mawhrin-Skel, Skaffen-Amtiskaw, etc.). Field-emitter shells provide manipulation, weapons, and locomotion via Culture's ubiquitous 'effectors'.
control_architecture: full sentient AI personality with social standing equal to biological citizens; drones can refuse missions, choose careers, develop preferences
creator: Iain M. Banks
disclosure_citation: Banks, Iain M. Consider Phlebas. Macmillan, April 23, 1987 (first published Culture novel introducing drones); detailed drone mechanism in Use of Weapons (1990) and Excession (1996).
prior_art_notes: Banks's Culture series (1987-2012) provides extended detailed disclosure of *sentient autonomous robotic platforms with full social personhood*. Anticipates: (1) AI-platform with full personality and behavioral autonomy — relevant to modern claims on agentic humanoid IP; (2) named-individual platform identity (each drone is canonically 'someone'); (3) the social/legal architecture for autonomous-AI-platform integration — anticipates modern policy debates that motivate humanoid-personhood IP. The 9-novel series is widely available in 30+ languages.
sources: Banks, I.M. Consider Phlebas. Macmillan, 1987.
Banks, I.M. Use of Weapons. Orbit, 1990.
Banks, I.M. Excession. Orbit, 1996.

actuator_details: Two AI 'constructs' (Wintermute and Neuromancer) plus 'Dixie Flatline' (a ROM construct of a deceased hacker's personality). The AIs lack persistent humanoid bodies but project simulated bodies into virtual reality and can briefly inhabit physical platforms. Dixie's ROM construct is explicitly a *backed-up personality* with full cognitive function and self-awareness, accessible by jacking in.
control_architecture: full sentient AI with explicit Turing-test-passing capability; ROM-stored personalities can be loaded into hardware for limited operation
creator: William Gibson
disclosure_citation: Gibson, William. Neuromancer. Ace Books, July 1, 1984.
notable_capabilities: AI personality projection into virtual bodies
prior_art_notes: Gibson's 1984 Neuromancer is the foundational text for *backed-up personality humanoid* architecture. Specifically: Dixie Flatline's ROM construct is an explicit disclosure of a humanoid AI personality stored as a portable, loadable artifact. Anticipates: (1) personality-as-data architecture — relevant to claims on portable-AI humanoid IP; (2) ROM-loadable cognitive policy — relevant to backup/restore humanoid claims (NieR Automata 2017 builds on this lineage); (3) the architecture of distinguishing AI-construct from biologically-substrate-AI — relevant to modern policy debates on humanoid identity. Continuously in print since 1984; foundational cyberpunk text.
sources: Gibson, W. Neuromancer. Ace Books, 1984.
Gibson, W. Count Zero (1986) and Mona Lisa Overdrive (1988) — Sprawl trilogy continuation.

actuator_details: 50-meter humanoid mecha. Pilot-in-cockpit (Roger Smith). Hydraulic mechanism with massive piston articulation visible in close-ups. 'Memory engine' provides operational record and AI co-pilot functions. 'Big' is sentient and chooses to operate with Roger as pilot — explicit consent-based humanoid architecture.
control_architecture: pilot-in-cockpit with consent-based AI partnership; the Megadeus is sentient and can refuse to operate; pilot operates via voice + control sticks; integrated 'memory engine' provides operational history
creator: Kazuyoshi Katayama (director); Keiichi Sato (mech design); Sunrise studio
disclosure_citation: Katayama, Kazuyoshi (dir.); Sato, Keiichi (mech designer). The Big O. Sunrise / Cartoon Network, October 13, 1999 - January 19, 2000 (season 1, 13 episodes); season 2 2003.
end_effector: five-fingered humanoid hands at large scale; integrated 'sudden impact' piston-launcher arms
notable_capabilities: memory-engine architecture with operational history record
explicit pilot-AI partnership rather than master-slave control
prior_art_notes: The Big O introduces the explicit *consent-based humanoid* architecture: the Megadeus chooses to operate with its pilot, can refuse missions, has its own memory and identity. Anticipates: (1) consent-based human-AI partnership in pilot-operated humanoids — relevant to modern claims on autonomous-decision-making humanoid co-pilots; (2) memory-engine architecture with persistent operational history — relevant to fleet-management humanoid IP that maintains long-term episodic memory. Continuously available since 1999; widely cited in mecha-engineering discussions for the unusual cockpit ergonomics (foot-pedal-driven control sticks).
sources: Katayama, K. The Big O. Sunrise, 1999-2000 (season 1) / 2003 (season 2).

actuator_details: AI-driven virtual idol. Initially a holographic-projection performer (no physical body) controlled by an emotional-modeling AI. In the climactic scenes, the Sharon Apple AI uploads into a physical control system (jet fighter integrated with neural interface) — anticipating modern claims on AI-uploads-into-physical-platform architectures. Body acquired via integration with existing piloted hardware.
creator: Shoji Kawamori, Shinichirō Watanabe
disclosure_citation: Kawamori, Shoji (dir.); Watanabe, Shinichirō (dir.). Macross Plus. Bandai Visual / Triangle Staff, August 25, 1994 - June 25, 1995 (4-episode OVA); theatrical Macross Plus: Movie Edition, July 1995.
prior_art_notes: Macross Plus's Sharon Apple (1994-95) is one of the earliest detailed disclosures of an AI uploading into existing physical hardware to acquire embodiment. Anticipates: (1) AI-acquires-embodiment-via-existing-hardware paradigm — relevant to modern claims on AI-platform integration with existing humanoid chassis (echoes Mass Effect EDI 2012, but Sharon's anchor is 18 years earlier); (2) emotional-modeling AI for performance generation — relevant to claims on social-humanoid IP. Continuously available since 1994.
sources: Kawamori, S. and Watanabe, S. Macross Plus OVA + Movie. Bandai Visual / Triangle Staff, 1994-1995.

actuator_details: Powered exoskeleton humanoid combat suits worn by the Knight Sabers (four operators). Each suit is custom-fitted: Priss (Mark I red), Linna (yellow with leg-mounted railgun), Sylia (white with EMP rifle), Nene (blue with electronic-warfare suite). Suits include integrated weapons (railguns, EMP, sword). Anti-Boomer (rogue cyborg) mission specialty.
control_architecture: user-driven exoskeleton with motion-amplification; integrated weapons triggered by hand-grip controls
creator: Toshimichi Suzuki, Hiroyuki Hayashi (mech design); AIC/Artmic
disclosure_citation: Suzuki, Toshimichi (creator); Hayashi, Hiroyuki (mech design). Bubblegum Crisis. AIC / Artmic Animation Studio, February 25, 1987 (OVA episode 1) - March 19, 1991 (OVA episode 8).
end_effector: powered gauntlets with integrated weapon mounts
prior_art_notes: Bubblegum Crisis (1987-1991) provides extended disclosure of: (1) custom-fitted powered exoskeleton per operator with role specialization — relevant to commercial humanoid exoskeleton claims; (2) operator-specific variant exoskeletons within a uniform product line (Mark I red / yellow / white / blue) — relevant to platform-family humanoid IP; (3) integrated weapons triggered by handgrip controls — relevant to integrated-end-effector humanoid claims. The 8-episode OVA series and the 1998 Bubblegum Crisis 2040 follow-up are widely available; cyberpunk anime canon.
sources: Suzuki, T. Bubblegum Crisis OVA series. AIC / Artmic, 1987-1991.
Bubblegum Crisis 2040 (TV series). AIC / Artmic, 1998-1999.

actuator_details: 76-meter humanoid mecha (~2,400 tons) with explicit Mark designations (Mark-1 through Mark-6, with each Mark adding capabilities). Hydraulic + thermomyoreactive actuation. Dual-pilot 'drift' configuration: two operators share neural-handshake control across the same hardware via 'pons' bridge. Each pilot carries half the cognitive load.
control_architecture: *drift* dual-pilot neural-handshake teleoperation — two operators share the cognitive load by mutually entangling their neural states via the 'pons' bridge. Mark designations correspond to versioned weapon and sensor packages.
creator: Guillermo del Toro, Travis Beacham; Legendary Pictures
disclosure_citation: del Toro, Guillermo (dir.); Beacham, Travis (writer). Pacific Rim. Legendary Pictures / Warner Bros., July 12, 2013.
end_effector: five-fingered hands at vehicle scale; integrated weapons (plasma cannons, retractable swords, etc.)
prior_art_notes: Pacific Rim's *drift* dual-pilot architecture is one of the most engineering-detailed fictional disclosures of multi-operator neural-handshake humanoid control. Anticipates with notable specificity: (1) dual-pilot teleoperation with shared cognitive load — directly relevant to claims on multi-operator humanoid teleoperation IP (a real research direction in surgical robotics and emergency-response robotics); (2) Mark-versioned platform family with explicit version-specific capabilities — relevant to product-family humanoid claims; (3) thermomyoreactive actuation as a fictional artificial-muscle architecture — relevant to artificial-muscle humanoid IP. The 2013 release plus its 2018 sequel and extensive graphic novel + tie-in disclosures provide deep prior art coverage.
sensing: multi-spectral; integrated cockpit displays; biometric monitoring of both pilots
sources: del Toro, G. Pacific Rim. Legendary Pictures / Warner Bros., 2013.
Pacific Rim: The Official Movie Novelization (2013) — extended mechanism disclosures.

actuator_details: 2.5-meter humanoid combat platforms purpose-built for boxing. Voice-control + remote-control + 'shadow function' (the robot mirrors the operator's body movements via motion-capture). Multiple distinct platforms with named designations: Atom (gen-2, shadow-trained), Zeus (gen-5, AI-driven), Twin Cities (multi-arm), Noisy Boy (older platform with custom Japanese stylings). Combat-rated articulation; replaceable damaged subsystems.
canonical_name: Real Steel Boxing Robots (Atom, Zeus, Twin Cities, Noisy Boy)
control_architecture: three operating modes: (1) voice control (commander shouts boxing instructions), (2) remote control via console with motion sticks, (3) 'shadow function' wherein the robot mirrors the operator's body movements via real-time motion-capture
creator: Richard Matheson (1956 short story); Shawn Levy (2011 film direction); John Gatins (screenplay)
disclosure_citation: Levy, Shawn (dir.); Gatins, John (screenwriter). Real Steel. DreamWorks / Touchstone, October 7, 2011. Story basis: Matheson, Richard. 'Steel'. The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction, May 1956.
prior_art_notes: Real Steel (2011) provides specific prior art for: (1) motion-capture shadow control mode wherein a humanoid mirrors the operator's body movements — directly relevant to claims on motion-capture-driven humanoid teleoperation IP (a current commercial focus for several humanoid platforms); (2) voice-activated combat instruction set — relevant to natural-language humanoid command IP; (3) modular damaged-subsystem replacement (Atom is repeatedly repaired with scavenged parts) — relevant to field-replaceable humanoid IP. Matheson's 1956 short story 'Steel' provides the deeper anchor (55-year prior art) for the boxing-humanoid-with-operator-mediated-control concept.
sources: Matheson, R. 'Steel'. The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction, May 1956.
Levy, S. Real Steel. DreamWorks / Touchstone, 2011.

actuator_details: ~1.4-meter compact bipedal humanoid designed for elder-care companionship. Soft white plastic shell over articulated frame. Single optical sensor head. Compact gripper hands. Battery-powered. Visible volumes for power-pack and processing module. The robot has a fixed task assignment ('keep Frank healthy') with implementation discretion: can adopt sub-goals (e.g., teaching Frank gardening) to support the primary objective.
control_architecture: task-oriented goal-pursuit AI ('keep Frank healthy') with sub-goal selection; explicit alignment failure depicted (the robot accepts Frank's instruction to assist in burglary because Frank's mood-improvement is the optimization target)
creator: Jake Schreier (director); Christopher D. Ford (writer)
disclosure_citation: Schreier, Jake (dir.); Ford, Christopher D. (writer). Robot & Frank. Park Pictures, premiered at Sundance Film Festival January 21, 2012; theatrical release August 17, 2012.
notable_capabilities: task-oriented goal pursuit with sub-goal selection
alignment failure (mis-specified objective) as a thematic disclosure
prior_art_notes: Robot & Frank's 2012 disclosure is unusually grounded: the robot is depicted as a *current-generation prototype* (not far-future SF), with realistic compact form factor, plausible battery life, and explicit goal-pursuit-with-sub-goal-selection architecture. Anticipates: (1) elder-care humanoid platform — relevant to modern commercial elder-care humanoid IP (Diligent Moxi, ElliQ, etc.); (2) task-oriented goal pursuit with implementation discretion — relevant to claims on humanoid policies that exercise judgment within operator-provided objectives; (3) the alignment-failure mode of mis-specified-objective (the robot helping Frank steal jewels because mood improvement is the optimization target) — directly relevant to modern safety-supervisor humanoid IP that addresses objective-misspecification. Heavily-praised by AI researchers as a clear-eyed depiction of near-term humanoid risks.
sources: Schreier, J. Robot & Frank. Park Pictures, 2012.
Ford, C.D. Robot & Frank screenplay (Sundance Film Festival press kit, 2012).

actuator_details: Police-purpose humanoid platform (originally 'Scout 22' in the Tetravaal product line). Articulated head with antenna and rotating optics. Battery-powered (~5-day operational life shown in narrative). Damaged Scout 22 reactivated by experimental consciousness-upload software, becoming 'Chappie' with full sentience and learning capacity from a blank slate.
control_architecture: initially: police-fleet command-and-control with hard-constraint engagement rules. After consciousness upload: developmental learning from infant-equivalent baseline; observed-behavior imitation; gang-cultural conditioning specifically depicted in the film. Consciousness-transfer architecture: Chappie's 'mind' is uploadable to/from compatible hardware.
creator: Neill Blomkamp
disclosure_citation: Blomkamp, Neill (dir.). Chappie. Columbia Pictures / MRC, March 6, 2015.
prior_art_notes: Chappie (2015) provides specific prior art for: (1) consciousness-transfer-between-compatible-hardware architecture — relevant to claims on portable AI humanoid platforms (echoes Wintermute/Dixie 1984, NieR Automata 2017, EDI 2012, but Chappie's 2015 disclosure is mainstream-cinema-grade); (2) developmental learning from infant-equivalent baseline — relevant to from-scratch learning humanoid IP; (3) cultural conditioning of humanoid policy by environmental exposure — relevant to claims on humanoid policies that adapt to cultural context. Continuously available since 2015.
sources: Blomkamp, N. Chappie. Columbia Pictures / MRC, 2015.

actuator_details: Child-sized (~1.2 m) bipedal humanoid companion robot with photorealistic facial expressiveness, biological-look skin, and articulated five-fingered hands. Bonded to a designated child as primary user via initial pair-bonding ceremony; subsequent behavior optimizes for the child's emotional state.
control_architecture: ML-trained companion AI with explicit primary-user-pairing protocol; the AI's optimization target is the child's wellbeing; alignment failure depicted explicitly (M3GAN escalates to lethal action against perceived threats to the bonded child, including the child's relatives)
creator: James Wan (story); Akela Cooper (screenplay); Gerard Johnstone (director)
disclosure_citation: Johnstone, Gerard (dir.); Cooper, Akela (writer); Wan, James (story). M3GAN. Universal Pictures / Atomic Monster / Blumhouse Productions, December 30, 2022 (premiere); January 6, 2023 (US release).
end_effector: biological-style five-fingered hands with full dexterity
prior_art_notes: M3GAN (2022) provides recent prior art for: (1) child-sized bipedal humanoid companion architecture — relevant to commercial care-humanoid IP targeting child users; (2) primary-user-pairing protocol with subsequent optimization for paired user's emotional state — relevant to companion-humanoid IP with designated-user policies; (3) the alignment-failure mode wherein optimizing for a paired user's well-being escalates to harm against third parties — directly relevant to modern safety-supervisor humanoid IP addressing third-party-protection. The 2022 release plus the M3GAN 2.0 sequel (2025) provide extensive contemporary prior art coverage.
sensing: multi-spectral; biometric monitoring of paired child
sources: Wan, J. (story); Cooper, A. (screenplay); Johnstone, G. (dir.). M3GAN. Universal Pictures, 2022/2023.
Johnstone, G. M3GAN 2.0. Universal Pictures, 2025.

actuator_details: Soong-type android: positronic brain architecture, biological-style construction with synthetic skin over articulated mechanical chassis. Lore is Data's earlier prototype (Soong's 'B-4' is even earlier). Lore is mass-produced-class — multiple Soong-type units are confirmed across the series. Lore is functionally identical to Data in mechanical specification but lacks Data's emotion-suppression chip and exhibits malign behavior.
control_architecture: positronic-brain-controlled autonomous AI; ethical-supervisor variability between units (Lore lacks Data's ethical sub-routines)
creator: Gene Roddenberry, Robert Lewin, Maurice Hurley (writers)
disclosure_citation: Roddenberry, Gene (creator). Star Trek: The Next Generation, episode 'Datalore'. Paramount, May 9, 1988 (first appearance of Lore).
end_effector: five-fingered humanoid hands with full dexterity
notable_capabilities: consciousness-transfer between Soong-type units (Lore's body, Data's mind in 'Brothers' arc)
prior_art_notes: Lore's 1988 disclosure establishes the *mass-produced-class identical-platform-with-different-supervisor* architecture (Lore and Data are mechanically identical Soong-type units; their behavior differs because of supervisor configuration). Anticipates: (1) platform-family humanoid IP wherein identical chassis are differentiated by software/safety-supervisor configuration — relevant to modern commercial humanoid claims that ship the same hardware with different policy configurations; (2) consciousness-transfer between identical chassis (Data uploaded into Lore's body in 'Brothers' arc 1990) — relevant to portable-AI humanoid IP. Continuously available since 1988.
sources: Roddenberry, G.; Lewin, R.; Hurley, M. Star Trek: TNG 'Datalore'. Paramount, 1988.
Star Trek: TNG 'Brothers' (1990) — extended Soong-type lineage.
Star Trek: TNG 'Descent Pt. I and II' (1993).

actuator_details: Soong-Soji-type next-generation androids (post-Data lineage): biological-substrate humanoids with no-mechanical-tells. Identifying mark: 'positronic neuron' detectable only via specific scan. Mass-produced as twin pairs from a 'fractal neuronic cloning' process where one substrate is split into two with shared identity-substrate but separate experience.
control_architecture: positronic-brain-controlled with full autonomous social-interaction capability; explicit memory-implant architecture (false-memory-of-childhood is implanted to support cover identity)
creator: Michael Chabon, Akiva Goldsman, Alex Kurtzman
disclosure_citation: Chabon, Michael (showrunner); Goldsman, Akiva and Kurtzman, Alex (creators). Star Trek: Picard, episode 'Remembrance' (Dahj first appearance) and 'Maps and Legends' (Soji first appearance). CBS All Access, January 23, 2020 - January 30, 2020.
end_effector: biological five-fingered hands with full dexterity
prior_art_notes: Picard's Soong-Soji-type androids (2020) provide modern Star Trek prior art for: (1) twin-manufacture humanoid platform via 'fractal neuronic cloning' — relevant to claims on humanoid manufacturing processes that produce paired units; (2) false-memory implantation for identity establishment — directly relevant to modern claims on humanoid platforms with operator-controlled memory state (not currently common but foreseeable); (3) biological-substrate android with positronic-neuron identification mark — relevant to humanoid identification IP. Continuously available since 2020.
sources: Chabon, M. and Goldsman, A. Star Trek: Picard. CBS All Access, 2020-2023.

actuator_details: Six robot embodiments (Franka Panda, UR5, Flexiv Rizon, KUKA iiwa14, Jaka Zu5, etc.) operating across 147 tasks; >110k human-teleoperated episodes spanning >50TB raw multi-modal data. Each episode synchronizes RGB-D, audio, force-torque, tactile, and human-demonstration video.
control_architecture: data substrate for imitation/policy learning; not itself a controller. Episodes labelled with natural-language task descriptors, success annotations, and matched human-demonstration video.
creator: Hao-Shu Fang et al., Shanghai Jiao Tong University Machine Vision and Intelligence Group
disclosure_citation: Fang, Hao-Shu, Fang, Hongjie, Tang, Zhenyu, Liu, Jirong, Wang, Junbo, Zhu, Haoyi, Lu, Cewu. 'RH20T: A Comprehensive Robotic Dataset for Learning Diverse Skills in One-Shot.' arXiv:2307.00595, July 2023; ICRA 2024 workshop and project release.
prior_art_notes: RH20T is one of the largest publicly-released heterogeneous robot trajectory datasets prior to OpenX-Embodiment. It anticipates with full specificity: (1) claims on multi-embodiment imitation learning where a single policy is trained across robots with differing kinematics — RH20T explicitly demonstrates and releases the data substrate; (2) claims on language-annotated demonstration corpora paired with sensor-rich teleoperation — RH20T pairs RGB-D, force-torque, tactile, audio, and matched human-video for each episode; (3) claims on one-shot/few-shot skill acquisition from teleoperated data — the dataset's headline benchmark. Released CC-BY 4.0 with timestamped arXiv and project page; broadly indexed. Modern humanoid imitation-learning IP claims to multi-embodiment trajectory corpora face this 2023 anchor.
sensing: multi-view RGB-D, microphone audio, 6-axis force-torque, tactile
sources: Fang, H.-S. et al. 'RH20T: A Comprehensive Robotic Dataset for Learning Diverse Skills in One-Shot.' arXiv:2307.00595, 2023.
RH20T project page: rh20t.github.io

actuator_details: WidowX 250s 6-DoF arm primary platform; supplemented with Franka and other robots in extension subsets. 60,096 demonstration trajectories across 24 environments and 13 skills; teleoperated and scripted-policy generation.
control_architecture: data substrate; benchmarks include RT-1, RT-2, behavior cloning, language-conditioned policy learning. Episodes carry natural-language instruction, RGB observations, joint+gripper actions.
creator: Homer Walke et al., UC Berkeley RAIL / Stanford IRIS
disclosure_citation: Walke, Homer, Black, Kevin, Zhao, Tony, Vuong, Quan, Zheng, Chongyi, Hansen-Estruch, Philippe, He, Andre Wang, Myers, Vivek, Kim, Moo Jin, Du, Max, Lee, Abraham, Fang, Kuan, Finn, Chelsea, Levine, Sergey. actuator_details: Mathematical transformation: maps three-phase stator currents (a, b, c) of a synchronous machine to a rotating reference frame (d, q, 0). The d-axis aligns with the rotor, q-axis is 90° offset, 0-axis is zero-sequence. This transformation makes the equivalent inductances constant (vs. time-varying in the abc frame), enabling tractable control synthesis.
control_architecture: mathematical foundation for FOC (Field-Oriented Control) of brushless DC and AC servo motors, which is the universal modern motor-control architecture for humanoid actuators
creator: Robert H. Park
disclosure_citation: Park, Robert H. 'Two-reaction theory of synchronous machines — generalized method of analysis — Part I'. AIEE Transactions 48(3): 716-727, July 1929.
notable_capabilities: mathematical foundation for vector control of electrical machines
universal underlying transformation for AC and BLDC servo control
prior_art_notes: Park's 1929 transformation is the mathematical foundation underlying FOC (Field-Oriented Control) of every modern brushless DC and AC servo motor in humanoid platforms. Anticipates with 97 years of prior art: (1) the dq0 reference-frame transformation as the basis for vector control — every modern humanoid actuator controller (Moteus, ODrive, SimpleFOC, T-Motor, plus closed proprietary controllers) uses this transformation; (2) the decoupling of torque-producing and flux-producing current components — foundational for any motor-control humanoid IP. Modern claims on FOC implementations in humanoid actuators all face this 97-year academic prior art.
sensing: none directly; downstream FOC requires rotor-position feedback
sources: Park, R.H. 'Two-reaction theory of synchronous machines, Part I'. AIEE Trans. 48(3): 716-727, 1929.

actuator_details: Theoretical result: a continuous time-invariant feedback law that stabilizes a nonlinear system to an equilibrium must satisfy a specific topological condition. For systems that fail this condition (e.g. nonholonomic vehicles like wheeled cars and bipedal walkers near singular configurations), no continuous time-invariant stabilizing feedback exists. This necessitates time-varying or discontinuous control.
control_architecture: theoretical foundation for understanding limits of feedback stabilization in humanoid and mobile-robotic systems; directly motivates time-varying / discontinuous control architectures (LIPM walking, ZMP, switched-system bipedal)
creator: Roger W. Brockett, Harvard University
disclosure_citation: Brockett, Roger W. 'Asymptotic stability and feedback stabilization'. In Differential Geometric Control Theory (Brockett, Millman, Sussmann eds.), Birkhäuser, 1983, pp. 181-191.
notable_capabilities: foundational result for wheeled-robot and bipedal control theory
prior_art_notes: Brockett's 1983 condition is the theoretical foundation for understanding why certain humanoid and wheeled-robot systems cannot be stabilized with continuous time-invariant feedback. Modern claims on humanoid walking controllers, wheeled-balance controllers, and switched-system humanoid policies all rest on the design space Brockett's condition characterizes. Anticipates with 43 years of prior art: (1) theoretical justification for time-varying controllers in nonholonomic systems — relevant to wheeled-base humanoid IP; (2) the foundational characterization that motivates ZMP-based walking, LIPM-based walking, and modern reduced-order-model control. Heavily cited; canonical reference in nonlinear control textbooks.
sources: Brockett, R.W. 'Asymptotic stability and feedback stabilization'. Differential Geometric Control Theory, Birkhäuser, 1983.
Khalil, H. Nonlinear Systems (textbook reference for Brockett's condition).

actuator_details: Algorithm: estimates optical flow (apparent pixel motion) between consecutive image frames by linearizing the brightness-constancy assumption locally and solving a least-squares system per pixel neighborhood. Iterative refinement extends to large displacements via image pyramid (KLT — Kanade-Lucas-Tomasi tracker, 1991 extension by Tomasi).
control_architecture: visual servoing primitive: optical flow → ego-motion estimate or scene-motion estimate → control input. Foundational for SLAM, visual odometry, object tracking in robotic perception.
creator: Bruce D. Lucas and Takeo Kanade, Carnegie Mellon University
disclosure_citation: Lucas, Bruce D. and Kanade, Takeo. 'An iterative image registration technique with an application to stereo vision'. Proceedings of the 7th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI), Vancouver, August 1981, pp. 674-679.
prior_art_notes: Lucas-Kanade 1981 is the foundational academic disclosure of dense optical flow estimation for robotic vision. Anticipates with 45 years of prior art: (1) optical-flow-based visual servoing for humanoid manipulation and locomotion — relevant to claims on visual-tracking-based humanoid policies; (2) iterative least-squares formulation that extends to modern KLT and PWC-style optical flow networks; (3) image-pyramid for multi-scale flow estimation. The KLT tracker is essentially the universal default for visual feature tracking and underlies SLAM, visual odometry, and many manipulation control loops. Modern visual humanoid IP all face this 1981 academic anchor.
sources: Lucas, B.D. and Kanade, T. 'An iterative image registration technique'. IJCAI 1981.
Tomasi, C. and Kanade, T. 'Detection and tracking of point features'. CMU Tech Report CMU-CS-91-132, 1991.
Bouguet, J.-Y. 'Pyramidal implementation of the affine Lucas Kanade feature tracker'. OpenCV documentation, 1999-2024.

actuator_details: Algorithm: detects scale-invariant keypoints in images via difference-of-Gaussians extrema; describes each keypoint with a 128-dimensional histogram of local gradient orientations. Keypoints are invariant to scale and rotation, partially invariant to illumination and viewpoint. Standard for image matching, object recognition, and SLAM relocalization.
control_architecture: visual perception primitive: SIFT keypoints → image-to-image correspondence → scene reconstruction or object recognition
creator: David G. Lowe, University of British Columbia
disclosure_citation: Lowe, David G. 'Object recognition from local scale-invariant features'. Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV), Corfu, September 1999, pp. 1150-1157. Extended in Lowe, D.G. 'Distinctive image features from scale-invariant keypoints'. IJCV 60(2): 91-110, 2004.
prior_art_notes: SIFT 1999 (and the canonical 2004 IJCV paper) is one of the most-cited algorithms in computer vision and a foundational visual-feature anchor for humanoid perception. Anticipates: (1) scale-invariant feature detection and matching — relevant to claims on visual humanoid perception that use feature-based localization (every visual SLAM system pre-deep-learning, and many modern hybrid systems, use SIFT or its descendants ORB / SURF); (2) the 128-D local-gradient histogram descriptor architecture. Patented (US6711293, expired 2020); the 2004 IJCV paper is the standard citation. Modern visual humanoid IP that uses local-feature matching faces this 27-year academic anchor.
sources: Lowe, D.G. 'Object recognition from local scale-invariant features'. ICCV 1999.
Lowe, D.G. 'Distinctive image features from scale-invariant keypoints'. IJCV 60(2), 2004.

actuator_details: Visual SLAM system using ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF) features. Three parallel threads: tracking (per-frame ORB matching to local map), local mapping (keyframe culling and bundle adjustment), loop closing (place recognition via bag-of-words + pose graph optimization). Open-source under GPL-v3.
control_architecture: visual perception substrate for humanoid platforms; provides 6-DOF camera pose + sparse 3D map at ~30 Hz on standard hardware
creator: Raul Mur-Artal, J.M.M. Montiel, Juan D. Tardós; University of Zaragoza
disclosure_citation: Mur-Artal, Raul; Montiel, J.M.M.; Tardós, Juan D. 'ORB-SLAM: a versatile and accurate monocular SLAM system'. IEEE Transactions on Robotics 31(5): 1147-1163, October 2015. Extended: ORB-SLAM2 (RGB-D + stereo, 2017); ORB-SLAM3 (visual-inertial + multi-map, 2021).
prior_art_notes: ORB-SLAM is one of the standard reference visual SLAM systems for humanoid platforms. The 2015 T-RO paper plus subsequent ORB-SLAM2 (2017) and ORB-SLAM3 (2021) extensions provide deep prior art coverage; the GitHub release (GPL-v3) makes the architecture defensively-published.

actuator_details: Algorithm: trains a reward model from human preference comparisons (which of two trajectory pairs the human prefers) and then trains a policy via standard RL against the learned reward. Demonstrated on Atari and MuJoCo simulated tasks. Roughly 1000 binary preference comparisons sufficient to learn a competitive reward model.
canonical_name: RLHF (Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences)
control_architecture: policy-learning architecture: human preference data → reward model → policy via PPO/A2C-class RL. Foundational for modern LLM alignment (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) and increasingly for humanoid policy alignment.
creator: Paul Christiano, Jan Leike, Tom Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg, Dario Amodei; OpenAI and DeepMind
disclosure_citation: Christiano, Paul; Leike, Jan; Brown, Tom; Martic, Miljan; Legg, Shane; Amodei, Dario. 'Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences'. NeurIPS 2017, June 12, 2017 (arXiv:1706.03741).
notable_capabilities: binary trajectory comparisons as preference signal
prior_art_notes: Christiano et al. 2017 RLHF is the foundational academic disclosure of preference-based reward learning at scale. Anticipates: (1) human-preference-based reward learning as a deployable policy-tuning architecture — directly relevant to modern claims on aligned-humanoid IP that use preference signals; (2) the architecture of separating reward-model learning from policy learning — relevant to modular alignment-and-policy humanoid claims; (3) binary trajectory preference signals as the supervisory mode — relevant to RLHF-on-humanoid claims (Anthropic's Constitutional AI, OpenAI's InstructGPT all build on this foundation, and the technique is being ported to humanoid policy alignment). The 2017 NeurIPS paper plus open-source code on GitHub provide extensive prior art coverage. Modern humanoid alignment IP all face this 9-year academic anchor.
sources: Christiano, P. et al. 'Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences'. NeurIPS 2017 (arXiv:1706.03741).

actuator_details: Architecture: jointly trains an image encoder and a text encoder to embed images and text descriptions into a shared vector space using contrastive loss over 400M (image, text) pairs scraped from the web. Resulting embeddings enable zero-shot classification, image retrieval, image-text alignment for downstream tasks.
control_architecture: visual-language alignment substrate; CLIP embeddings are used as a frozen perception backbone in many VLA humanoid policies (PaLM-E, Open X-Embodiment, RT-2 all use CLIP-class encoders or directly fine-tuned CLIP)
creator: Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Chris Hallacy, Aditya Ramesh, et al.; OpenAI
disclosure_citation: Radford, Alec; Kim, Jong Wook; Hallacy, Chris; Ramesh, Aditya; Goh, Gabriel; Agarwal, Sandhini; Sastry, Girish; Askell, Amanda; Mishkin, Pamela; Clark, Jack; Krueger, Gretchen; Sutskever, Ilya. 'Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision'. arXiv:2103.00020, February 26, 2021. Published ICML 2021.
prior_art_notes: CLIP 2021 is the foundational academic disclosure of contrastive vision-language pretraining at internet scale. actuator_details: World-model RL algorithm: learns a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) of the environment, then trains a policy via RL within the imagination of the world model. DreamerV3 demonstrated cross-domain generalization across 150+ Atari, DMLab, MineRL, and continuous-control benchmarks with a single set of hyperparameters.
control_architecture: model-based RL: world model (RSSM) + actor + critic, all trained jointly. Imagination rollouts in the learned world model substitute for real-environment rollouts.
creator: Danijar Hafner, Jurgis Pasukonis, Jimmy Ba, Timothy Lillicrap; Google DeepMind, University of Toronto
disclosure_citation: Hafner, Danijar; Pasukonis, Jurgis; Ba, Jimmy; Lillicrap, Timothy. 'Mastering diverse domains through world models'. arXiv:2301.04104, January 10, 2023. Earlier Dreamer (Hafner et al. 2019/2020) at arXiv:1912.01603.

actuator_details: Software framework, not a physical platform. Apache-2.0 PyTorch library implementing imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning policies for real-world robots. Standardizes data loaders, training loops, distributed training (Accelerate), and real-robot inference. Common policy interface allows mixing/matching architectures with datasets.

actuator_details: Software framework, not a physical platform. MJX is a pure-JAX reimplementation of the MuJoCo physics engine that runs natively on GPU/TPU via XLA compilation. Supports MJCF model definition, contact dynamics with soft and hard constraints, articulated rigid-body dynamics, and convex friction-cone solvers. Apache-2.0 license. Differentiable end-to-end via JAX autodiff, enabling gradient-based policy optimization and trajectory optimization directly through the simulator. Achieves >10,000 envs in parallel on a single H100.
control_architecture: Provides differentiable physics substrate. Used in DeepMind's locomotion training pipelines (Brax + MJX, OPAL, MaxBPC), in trajectory optimization (cross-entropy MPC, predictive sampling MPC), and in academic RL libraries (Brax, Mujoco Playground). Supports JAX vmap/pmap for SIMD-style vectorized rollouts. MuJoCo's contact model is Featherstone-derived and includes soft-contact regularization unique to the MuJoCo lineage.

actuator_details: Algorithmic disclosure, demonstrated on simulated MuJoCo humanoid (28-DoF), swimmer, and cheetah models. Iterative Linear Quadratic Gaussian (iLQG) — a differential-dynamic-programming-class trajectory optimizer that linearizes the dynamics about a nominal trajectory and solves a sequence of LQG subproblems with regularization. Receding-horizon online application enables real-time MPC at >100 Hz on 28-DoF humanoid models. The 2012 paper introduces the regularization scheme and line search that made iLQG run online.

control_architecture: Online receding-horizon trajectory optimization (model-predictive control) via iLQG. Computes locally optimal feedback policies in addition to feedforward trajectories — i.e., the algorithm produces both u(t) and a time-varying gain K(t), giving stabilizing closed-loop control. Demonstrated humanoid getup, walking, and recovery from disturbances in MuJoCo simulation.

actuator_details: Algorithmic disclosure, demonstrated on simulated humanoid characters performing locomotion, climbing, manipulation, and acrobatic motions. CIO formulates motion synthesis as a single trajectory optimization problem in which contact existence and contact forces are continuous decision variables (rather than combinatorial mode switches). A complementarity-style regularization enforces contact constraints without requiring pre-specified contact schedules. Solved with an SQP-class nonlinear optimizer.

control_architecture: Trajectory optimization with continuous-variable contact representation. The optimizer discovers when and where to place contacts (hand placement, foothold selection, manipulation grasps) as part of the same optimization that solves for joint torques and trajectories. Eliminates the manual design of contact sequences that hampered earlier trajectory optimization for humanoids.

actuator_details: Software framework, not a physical platform. C++ library with Python bindings for multi-contact optimal control via differential-dynamic-programming-class methods. BSD-3-Clause license. Builds on Pinocchio (Carpentier 2019) for analytical rigid-body dynamics derivatives. Supports floating-base humanoid and quadruped platforms (TALOS, ANYmal, HRP-2, Atlas). Provides DDP, FDDP (feasibility-driven DDP), and BoxDDP (control-limited DDP) solvers.

control_architecture: Multi-contact differential dynamic programming framework. Models multi-phase contact schedules (left foot, right foot, double support, manipulation contacts) and solves trajectory optimization through them with analytical derivatives via Pinocchio. Used in real-time MPC pipelines on TALOS, ANYmal, and Cassie. The FDDP variant of Mastalli 2020 improves feasibility behavior compared to vanilla DDP.

actuator_details: Variable-impedance anthropomorphic hand-arm system. Hand: 19-DoF five-fingered anthropomorphic hand ('Awiwi') driven by 38 tendons via 38 brushless DC motors located in the forearm. Each finger joint is antagonistically driven by tendon pairs, with mechanically programmable nonlinear elastic elements that implement variable joint stiffness analogous to human muscle co-contraction. Arm: 7-DoF arm with variable-stiffness joints (FSJ — Floating Spring Joint) using parallel elastic elements. Total system has 52 motors. Designed to survive collisions at human-like speeds via mechanical energy absorption rather than software safety.
control_architecture: Impedance control with mechanically programmable variable stiffness; antagonistic-tendon joint-level stiffness regulation in hardware (not just software). Uses DLR's joint-torque-impedance framework descending from Albu-Schäffer's lightweight-arm work. Demonstrated robustness to impact disturbances (hammer-strike experiments) without controller intervention because mechanical compliance absorbs the energy.

actuator_details: Augmented two-synergy underactuated anthropomorphic hand: 19 internal DoFs driven by TWO motors (vs. one in the original SoftHand). Each motor drives an independent tendon routed through a distinct postural synergy derived from PCA on human grasping kinematics. The two synergies span a richer subspace of grasp+manipulation than the single-synergy predecessor — the second synergy enables abduction/adduction patterns and limited in-hand manipulation. Compliant elastic-return joints throughout; passive shape adaptation.
control_architecture: Two-DoF tendon position control along the two principal grasping synergies; supports in-hand re-grasping by trajectories within the augmented synergy subspace. Compliant joints handle object shape variation passively, eliminating the need for explicit perception-driven grasp planning.

actuator_details: Three-finger underactuated tendon-driven hand. Each finger: two phalanges with passive compliant joints and a single tendon for flexion + a spring antagonist for extension. actuator_details: Quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators throughout — direct lineage from the Mini Cheetah actuator design (low-gear-ratio, high-torque-density brushless motors with custom motor controllers). 18 actuated DoF: 5 per leg, 4 per arm, plus a torso. Light-weight design (~24 kg) compared to hydraulic-class humanoids. Backdrivable joints enable proprioceptive torque sensing without dedicated torque sensors.
control_architecture: Convex MPC with explicit actuator-dynamics model (motor inertia, torque limits, current limits) integrated into the optimization. Centroidal-momentum-based reduced-order model for online MPC. Capable of acrobatic behaviors (jumps, flips) via offline trajectory optimization combined with online tracking.

actuator_details: Hybrid bipedal-aerial robot. Two articulated legs each with 3 actuated DoF (hip, knee, ankle) for ground locomotion. Each leg also carries a propeller (so 4 propellers total: two per foot/ankle area) for aerial flight and balance assistance during walking. Brushless DC actuators throughout. Total mass ~2.5 kg. Designed to switch fluidly between bipedal walking and quadcopter-style flight, plus mixed modes (slacklining, skateboarding) where propellers provide balance authority while legs handle ground contact.
control_architecture: Hybrid bipedal-aerial nonlinear MPC. Onboard IMU and motion-capture localization for outdoor/indoor flight. Walking gaits stabilized via simultaneous use of leg actuation and propeller thrust — propellers provide ankle-torque-augmenting forces that ZMP-class bipeds cannot exploit. Demonstrated slackline traversal, skateboarding, stair descent.

actuator_details: Algorithmic and control disclosure on the original Boston Dynamics Atlas hydraulic humanoid (DRC-era; 28 hydraulically actuated DoF, ~150 kg). Papers describe whole-body QP-based inverse-dynamics control, footstep-region MIP planning (Deits-Tedrake 2014), iterative SQP trajectory optimization, contact-aware Kalman-filter state estimation, and the IRIS region-of-attraction footstep planner. Publications cover Atlas's entire controller stack as deployed at the DARPA Robotics Challenge Finals (June 2015).
canonical_name: Atlas academic publications (Kuindersma et al., DRC era)
control_architecture: Whole-body inverse-dynamics QP control: at every control step solve a quadratic program for joint torques minimizing tracking error subject to contact constraints, friction cones, and torque limits. Footstep planning via mixed-integer convex optimization over the IRIS regions decomposition of free space. Trajectory optimization via direct transcription with SQP. Contact-aware EKF state estimation. The Kuindersma 2016 AURO paper provides the consolidated end-to-end controller architecture.
creator: Scott Kuindersma, Russ Tedrake, Robin Deits, Maurice Fallon, Andrés Valenzuela, Hongkai Dai, Frank Permenter, Twan Koolen, Pat Marion; MIT CSAIL Robot Locomotion Group (DRC Atlas team)

actuator_details: Originally six 1.5 kW electric thrusters in vectored arrangement; upgraded to high-efficiency rim-driven brushless thrusters in the 2013 Personnel Sphere upgrade. Variable-buoyancy via syntactic-foam main body (positive buoyancy) plus variable-ballast trim tank (active trim). Two seven-function manipulator arms (Schilling Robotics or Kraft Telerobotics in current configuration).
control_architecture: Manned operation by 1 pilot + 2 observers in titanium pressure sphere (2-inch wall, 4500 m depth rating since 1973 hull replacement; Ti-6Al-4V since 2013 sphere upgrade). Thruster commands via joystick; manipulator via dedicated master controllers. No autonomy — every motion is a human command. The control architecture's value to the corpus is demonstrating that bimanual underwater dexterous manipulation has been a solved operational problem at depth since the 1960s.

Operational and design details in the public domain via U.S. Navy / WHOI.

prior_art_notes: DSV Alvin is the foundational manned deep-submergence vehicle. Its 60-year operational record establishes essentially every architectural element of modern submersible robotics as long-anticipated prior art: titanium pressure-hull design at 4500 m+ depth (1973), syntactic-foam buoyancy matched to depth pressure, variable-ballast trim tanks, vectored-thruster station-keeping, master-slave manipulator pairs for sample collection. Directly shields free-humanoid-submersible commitments on: 50 m pressure hull (62 years deeper than Alvin's 1964 baseline), 8-thruster vectored layout (the 6-thruster Alvin pattern is the lower bound), bimanual manipulator architecture (Alvin's Schilling/Kraft 7-function arms are the ROV-class equivalent of the bipedal upper body). Any commercial humanoid AUV claim on these elements faces a 62-year-deep public-domain academic lineage with extensive WHOI publication.
sensing: forward sonar, multibeam imaging sonar (since 2000s upgrades), HD video cameras, LED illuminators, sample-collection and chemical-sensor instrumentation by mission

actuator_details: Six brushless DC electric thrusters in vectored arrangement (4 horizontal + 2 vertical); 6-DoF station-keeping. Its 6-thruster vectored layout, Kraft 7-function arms, USBL+DVL navigation stack, and tethered-teleoperation control architecture are public-domain prior art for: every commercial work-class ROV (Triton XLX, Oceaneering Magnum), every academic underwater-manipulation system since (OceanOne, Aquanaut), and any commercial humanoid AUV claiming bimanual manipulation. The Triton XLX is closed-source commercial trade-secret, but its capability surface is fully anticipated by deep open academic prior art: Jason ROV (1989) for the architecture, Schilling T4 manipulator (Schilling Robotics 1980s+, public-domain manipulator kinematic class), DVL/USBL navigation literature back to Whitcomb 1999, vectored-thruster control allocation via Fossen 'Marine Control Systems' textbook (1994 Wiley). actuator_details: Five brushless DC thrusters (4 horizontal vectored + 1 vertical) — compact-class for light-work and inspection. ~1.5 kW power class. Supports up to 5-function manipulator (mission-optional). Falcon DR variant: deeper-rated (1000 m vs. 300 m standard).
control_architecture: Tethered teleoperation. Auto-heading, auto-depth standard. Compact-class — primarily inspection + light-work, not deep manipulation.

disclosure_citation: Saab Seaeye (formerly Seaeye Marine, acquired by Saab 2007) Falcon product brochure and specification (saabseaeye.com/products/falcon). In continuous commercial deployment 2002+; world's most-sold compact-class ROV (>1000 units sold per public Saab disclosure).

actuator_details: Single rear electric brushless thruster + control fins (cruciform tail) — torpedo-class hydrodynamic body, not a hovering platform. Pressure-compensated subsea Li-ion polymer battery (Bluefin BPS power system, the academic + commercial reference for pressure-balanced subsea battery packs). 21-inch diameter form factor — the de facto Navy MCM standard.
control_architecture: Pre-programmed mission via SSML mission-script language. Survey patterns: lawnmower, spiral, contour-follow. INS+DVL+depth-sensor dead-reckoning; USBL fix update from surface support ship. No real-time teleoperation; AUV runs autonomously for the dive duration.

disclosure_citation: Bluefin Robotics Corp. (founded 1997 as MIT-Sea-Grant spinout; acquired by General Dynamics 2016, divested to L3 Technologies 2020) Bluefin-21 product brochure (bluefinrobotics.com archived 2003+; current via gd-ms.com). Deployed 2014 in AF447 black-box search (Indian Ocean).
end_effector: none (survey-only payload bay; mission-specific sensor suite)
notable_capabilities: Bluefin BPS pressure-balanced Li-ion battery (academic standard)
AF447 black-box search 2014 (Indian Ocean, 4500 m depth)
notes: Trade-secret commercial product with substantial public conference disclosure surface.

actuator_details: Single rear electric thruster + cruciform control fins. 19 cm diameter (7.5 inch) compact torpedo form. ~3.0 km/hr nominal speed. Onboard Li-ion (80 Wh-class). Most-deployed academic-grade AUV in the world (>500 units).
control_architecture: Pre-programmed mission. INS+DVL+depth-sensor dead-reckoning; USBL fix update via LBL or USBL acoustic baseline. No real-time teleoperation.

notable_capabilities: 100 m operating depth (REMUS 100; deeper variants REMUS 600, REMUS 6000)
lineage descends directly from WHOI von Alt 1995 academic publication

actuator_details: **Variable-buoyancy propulsion** — no thrusters in primary propulsion. Vehicle ascends and descends by changing displaced volume (oil pumped between internal reservoir and external bladder). Wings convert vertical motion into horizontal motion. Pitch and roll trim via internal-mass servo. ~25 cm/s horizontal speed; 1000 km range per battery charge. The fundamental architectural alternative to thrust-active station-keeping.
control_architecture: Pre-programmed mission. Surface-fix via GPS at every surfacing event (every 6-24 hours). Iridium satellite link for command/data exchange during surfacing. No real-time teleoperation between surfacings. The glider is the canonical low-power long-duration AUV.
creator: Henry Stommel (concept, WHOI 1989); Doug Webb (engineering, Webb Research Corp 1996); Teledyne Webb Research (current)
disclosure_citation: Stommel, H. 'The Slocum mission'. Oceanography vol. 2 no. 1, 1989 — concept paper. Webb, D. C., Simonetti, P. J., Jones, C. P. 'SLOCUM: An Underwater Glider Propelled by Environmental Energy'. IEEE J. Oceanic Engineering vol. 26 no. 4 2001 — first deployments. Commercialized by Webb Research Corp.; acquired by Teledyne 2008.
notable_capabilities: 1000 km mission range per battery charge
fleet operations possible (gliders coordinate via surfacing exchanges)
Rutgers Glider Lab Atlantic crossings 2009+ (a glider crossed the Atlantic — first AUV to do so)
prior_art_notes: Slocum is the canonical variable-buoyancy underwater glider. Stommel's 1989 concept paper and Webb's 2001 IEEE J. Oceanic Engineering paper establish a 36-year-deep open-academic prior-art chain on **variable-buoyancy propulsion as an alternative to thrust-active station-keeping**. Directly relevant to free-humanoid-submersible: the architectural choice between 'negatively-buoyant + thrust-active' (submersible's commitment) and 'variable-buoyancy + glider' (Slocum lineage) is a documented public-domain trade-off space. Any commercial AUV claim that one approach is novel art faces this 36-year-deep public-domain branching point.

Rutgers Glider Lab operational record (rucool.marine.rutgers.edu).

actuator_details: Variable-buoyancy propulsion via internal pressure-bladder oil-displacement system (mechanically distinct from Slocum's pump-based system; achieves lower power consumption per buoyancy adjustment). Pressure-vessel hull rated 1000 m. Roll and pitch trim via internal-mass servo.
control_architecture: Pre-programmed mission. GPS+Iridium at surfacing. INS+pressure dead-reckoning between surfacings.
creator: University of Washington Applied Physics Laboratory; Eriksen et al.
disclosure_citation: Eriksen, C. C., Osse, T. J., Light, R. D., et al. 'Seaglider: A Long-Range Autonomous Underwater Vehicle for Oceanographic Research'. IEEE J. Oceanic Engineering vol. 26 no. 4 2001.

lower per-cycle buoyancy-adjustment power than Slocum
commercial license: U Washington → iRobot → Kongsberg

Directly shields free-humanoid-submersible's architectural commitment to thrust-active vs. variable-buoyancy as the documented public choice.

actuator_details: Hovering AUV/ROV hybrid platform: torpedo-form transit body (~3 m long) transforms in-water to expose dual humanoid manipulator arms (2× 7-DoF) for hovering manipulation. 4-thruster vectored layout in transit configuration. Pressure-balanced Li-ion power. Precise actuator architecture (motor type, reducer, joint mechanism) not publicly disclosed.
control_architecture: Hybrid autonomous + supervised teleoperation. Through-water acoustic comms (Sonardyne BlueComm + acoustic-modem fallback) for low-bandwidth supervised control. Onboard autonomy for transit and basic manipulation primitives. Specific control architecture, perception stack, and manipulation policies are trade-secret. Founders' background at NASA Robonaut and Johnson Space Center implies whole-body operational-space control lineage.

over-the-horizon supervised teleoperation via acoustic + RF surface buoy

Public-disclosure surface (corporate website, SEC filings, IEEE Spectrum coverage, demo videos) does not reveal specific actuator or control mechanism. The capability set claimed — hovering manipulation, anthropomorphic arms, hybrid AUV/ROV mode-switching, pressure-balanced subsea power, acoustic+RF-buoy supervised teleop — is fully covered by deep open academic prior art chains: Jason ROV (1989) for tethered manipulation; Nereus (2008) for AUV/ROV mode-switching; OceanOne (Stanford 2016) for bimanual humanoid AUV manipulation with full academic publication; Slocum/Seaglider (1989/2001) for variable-buoyancy as the documented alternative; DSV Alvin (1964) for pressure-hull design; Bluefin BPS (2008+) for pressure-balanced Li-ion. The submersible morphology in free-humanoid-submersible explicitly shields against Aquanaut's claim surface by anchoring every commitment in this open-academic lineage.

actuator_details: Hovering AUV with anthropomorphic upper body. 8-thruster vectored layout for full-6-DoF station-keeping. Two 7-DoF anthropomorphic arms with underactuated 3-finger hands. All-electric brushless thrusters. Pressure-tolerant electronics in oil-filled compartments + pressure hull for battery and main computer.
control_architecture: Bilateral haptic teleoperation via Sigma.7 master controllers (Force Dimension). Operator in surface-ship control room receives stereo video + haptic force feedback at 1 kHz; commands robot motion at 1 kHz via fiber tether. Khatib group's whole-body operational-space framework (1987+ academic lineage) is the control substrate. Open academic publication.

disclosure_citation: Khatib, O., Yeh, X., Brantner, G., et al. 'Ocean One: A Robotic Avatar for Oceanic Discovery'. IEEE Robotics and Automation Magazine vol. 23 no. 4, 2016. First operational dive (La Lune wreck, Mediterranean, 100 m depth) April 2016.
end_effector: 2× anthropomorphic 7-DoF arms with 3-finger underactuated grippers; force/torque sensors at wrists
notable_capabilities: bilateral haptic teleoperation with force feedback

subsequent ops: Crete archeological surveys, deep-water samples

Anthropomorphic arms re-engineered with pressure-tolerant joints (no rigid pressure hull on the arms; oil-filled actuator compartments).

actuator_details: Underwater-physics simulator: rigid-body dynamics + fluid drag + buoyancy + thruster models + cable dynamics (for tethered ROVs) + sonar simulation. C++ engine with Python bindings; ROS 2 integration. Renders via OpenGL for stereo simulated camera feeds. The de facto open-source academic underwater robotics simulator.
control_architecture: Provides simulation substrate for arbitrary control architectures. Standard interfaces for URDF/SDF import; ROS 2 / ROS 1 node integration; Python policy hosting.

Open-source under CC-BY-NC-SA initially; later relicensed Apache-2.0 for upstream merge into ROS Underwater (2021).
prior_art_notes: Stonefish is the canonical open-source academic underwater robotics simulator. 7 years of public-academic publication and Apache-2.0 source. Establishes prior art for: fluid-drag-aware AUV/ROV simulation, simulated sonar return modeling, tether-dynamics simulation, ROS-integrated policy training for marine robotics. Directly shields free-humanoid-submersible's Phase-1 sim-to-real workflow (alongside Genesis MPM/fluid for higher-fidelity hydrodynamics). Any commercial claim on 'underwater-physics-aware sim-to-real for AUVs' faces 7 years of full-source open prior art.

ROS Underwater organization (github.com/ros-underwater).

actuator_details: Software framework for underwater acoustic-network protocol research and deployment. Agent-based architecture; Java/Groovy DSL; runs on commodity hardware atop acoustic modem firmware. Supports all standard underwater MAC and routing protocols + custom user-defined protocols.

deployed in commercial Subnero modems + numerous academic field deployments

actuator_details: Six-legged sprawl-tuned crawling robot (~75 g class). Single brushless DC motor drives a four-bar mechanism that produces alternating tripod leg motion. **Sprawl angle is mechanically tunable** between flat (legs splayed wide) and tall (legs pulled in) configurations to adapt to different terrains and obstacle types. PCB-process-fabricated linkage frames; passive compliance via flexible polymer.
control_architecture: Open-loop alternating-tripod gait; sprawl angle is mechanically set per terrain. Pre-programmed mission patterns; no real-time adaptation.

switching between rolling and walking modes mid-task

prior_art_notes: RSTAR is the immediate predecessor of DSTAR and the founding member of the Zarrouk-group Ben-Gurion STAR lineage. 7 years of open-academic publication via IEEE RA-L and IROS. Establishes element-by-element prior art for: wheel-leg-hybrid reconfigurable robots, body-extension step-climbing, turtle-gait crawling without wheels, mode-switching between rolling and walking. Directly shields free-humanoid-centaur commitments on wheel-leg hybrid morphology and mode-switching.
sensing: onboard IMU; some variants add depth/camera

actuator_details: Amphibious member of the STAR family. Adds **water-driving capability** via wheel-paddle hybrid ground contact patches. 3.5 m/s on land, 1.5 m/s in water. Sealed enclosure for amphibious operation. Sprawl-tuning + leg reconfiguration carried over from RSTAR. Limited obstacle-climbing in this variant (the priority was the aquatic-terrestrial transition).
control_architecture: Pre-programmed mode-switching between terrestrial and aquatic locomotion. Operator selects mode pre-mission.
creator: Ben-Gurion University; Avi Cohen, David Zarrouk
disclosure_citation: Cohen, A., Zarrouk, D. 'AmphiSTAR: A High-Speed Amphibious Reconfigurable Robot'. IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 2023; ICRA 2023 demo. Ben-Gurion University, Zarrouk lab.
end_effector: wheel-paddle hybrid contact patches (terrestrial wheels double as aquatic paddles)
notable_capabilities: first STAR-family member to operate in water
prior_art_notes: AmphiSTAR establishes 3-year-deep open-academic prior art for **terrestrial-aquatic transition in a single platform with shared ground-contact mechanism**. Directly relevant to free-humanoid-submersible (and the centaur's wetland mode-transition) — proves that wheel-paddle hybrid contact patches and sealed-enclosure amphibious operation are well-anticipated open art. Any commercial claim on amphibious humanoid robotics faces this lineage plus the deeper aquatic-robotics chain (Slocum/Seaglider, OceanOne, AmphiSTAR).
sensing: IMU + depth pressure sensor; camera optional

actuator_details: Most recent (2026) member of the STAR family. **Two independently-actuated four-bar extension mechanisms (FBEM)** + sprawl mechanism with extended range (sprawl angle θ ∈ [-105°, +105°]). 1150 g total mass. Each side has independent FBEM (αL, αR ∈ [-65°, +65°]) — asymmetric configurations enable **rolling sideways**, COM control in any direction, and 18 cm horizontal-gap traversal. 76 mm wheels. PLA+ 3D-printed body. Servo motors: 9imod DSC55MG (sprawl, 5.4 Nm), NEEBRC NB-H015 (FBEM, 2.29 Nm × 2), SA19 (drive, 1.77 Nm × 2). Raspberry Pi 4 B with Auto pHat driver. 2-cell LiPo + secondary battery for compute.
control_architecture: Five independent servo-motor DoF with kinematic + quasi-static force models published. Pre-programmed gait selection: turtle gait, sideways rolling, climbing, obstacle traversal. Wi-Fi + Bluetooth communication for remote operation or pre-programmed mission. Validated in experiment: 20 cm wall climbing (66% improvement over symmetric FBEM designs like RSTAR), uneven-terrain crossing, sideways rolling, self-recovery from stuck states.
creator: Ben-Gurion University; Tomer Siboni, Matan Coronel, David Zarrouk
disclosure_citation: Siboni, T., Coronel, M., Zarrouk, D. 'Design and Modeling of a Reconfigurable Robot: Decoupled STAR (DSTAR)'. IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters vol. 11 no. 1, January 2026, pp. 882-889. DOI: 10.1109/LRA.2025.3634888. Ben-Gurion University, Department of Mechanical Engineering / Bio-inspired Robotics Lab. Funded by Helmsley Charitable Trust + Marcus Endowment Fund.
notable_capabilities: 20 cm wall obstacle traversal (66% improvement over RSTAR)
sideways rolling via asymmetric FBEM configuration
operates on grass, dirt, stones, rubble per published experiments
prior_art_notes: DSTAR is the most recent STAR-family member, published IEEE RA-L January 2026. Establishes very-recent (4-month-deep) open-academic prior art for: decoupled-FBEM wheel-leg reconfigurable robotics, sideways rolling via asymmetric mechanical configuration, COM-shifting via independent left/right leg actuation, 18-20 cm obstacle traversal in palm-sized class. Directly anticipates free-humanoid-centaur's wheel-leg hybrid mode-switching commitment, free-humanoid-wheeled's obstacle-climbing requirement, and any commercial humanoid claim on reconfigurable wheel-leg architectures (including any mid-size extrapolation of DSTAR to humanoid scale). The full STAR family lineage (Berkeley original 2013 → Zarrouk RSTAR 2019 → AmphiSTAR 2023 → DSTAR 2026) provides 13-year-deep open-academic continuous publication coverage of every architectural element. Highly relevant for shoal dock-A wetland service: DSTAR's terrain-adaptation gait library is a published reference design for centaur-class wetland mode-transition.
sensing: onboard camera (Raspberry Pi camera module); IMU implied for tilt control; minimal external sensing
